stimuli.title: A bite in the dark
stimuli.content:
Every year, thousands of people in rural India die after being bitten by snakes, and many more are left with damaged limbs. Most of the victims are farmers and farm workers, bitten while cutting crops, walking along field bunds at night or sleeping on the floor of their huts. The monsoon months, when rain floods the burrows of rats and drives out the snakes that hunt them, are the most dangerous.

Doctors say that most of these deaths can be prevented. An effective medicine, antivenom, has been available for decades and is produced in India. It works best when it is given early, ideally within a few hours of the bite. The tragedy is that many victims never reach a hospital in time.

One reason is distance. A village may be an hour or more from the nearest health centre that stocks antivenom. Another is belief. Many families first take the victim to a local healer, who may cut the wound, apply herbs or tie a tight cloth above the bite. Precious hours are lost, and some of these treatments cause harm of their own.

Health workers are trying to change this through simple advice. A person who has been bitten should stay calm and keep the bitten limb still, because movement helps the venom spread through the body. Rings and bangles should be removed before the limb swells. The victim should be carried, not made to walk, to a hospital as quickly as possible. Trying to suck out the venom or cutting the wound does no good.

Prevention matters too. Wearing boots in the fields, carrying a torch at night and sleeping on a raised cot rather than on the floor greatly reduce the risk. These are small habits, but in a country where snakes and people share the same fields, they can be the difference between life and death.

stimuli.title: Homes without an address
stimuli.content:
Ask for directions in many Indian towns and you will hear something like this: 'Go past the temple, turn left at the big neem tree, and ask for the house with the blue gate behind the flour mill.' For the people who live there, such directions work well enough. For anyone else, they can be a puzzle.

Millions of homes have no precise address. Streets may have no names, house numbers may be missing or follow no order, and the same name may be shared by two or three lanes. Local residents rarely notice the problem, because they know their neighbourhood by heart. It becomes serious only when a stranger must find a particular door quickly.

An ambulance driver is the most obvious example. Every minute he spends asking shopkeepers for directions is a minute lost for the patient. Fire engines and police vans face the same difficulty. Delivery companies also lose money: a parcel that cannot be delivered must be carried back, stored and sent out again, and some of that cost is passed on to customers.

The lack of an address can also shut people out. Opening a bank account, getting a gas connection or applying for a loan usually requires proof of where one lives. A family in an unnamed lane may find it hard to supply such proof, even if it has lived there for twenty years.

Several solutions are being tried. Some towns are naming streets and fixing number plates on every building. Others are testing digital codes that identify a small square of land from map coordinates, so that any location can be described by a short string of letters and numbers, even where there are no street names at all. Such codes do not depend on local knowledge, but they work only if people know their own code and the services that need it can read it.

An address, in short, is more than a line on an envelope. It is a way of being found.

stimuli.title: The first number in the room
stimuli.content:
In a well-known kind of experiment, people are asked to write down the last two digits of their phone number and then to say how much they would pay for an ordinary item, such as a box of chocolates or a cordless mouse. The digits have nothing to do with the item, and everyone knows it. Yet, again and again, those whose digits are high offer noticeably more than those whose digits are low. A number that should carry no weight has quietly pulled their judgement towards itself.

Psychologists call this anchoring. When we must estimate a value we are unsure of, we tend to start from whatever figure is in front of us and adjust from there, usually not far enough. The first number becomes an anchor, and our final answer stays within reach of its chain.

Sellers have long understood this. A shop that marks a sari at ₹6,000 and then 'reduces' it to ₹4,500 is not only offering a discount; it is fixing ₹6,000 in the buyer's mind as the true value, so that ₹4,500 feels like a gain, whatever the sari is really worth. In negotiations, too, the side that names the first figure often gains an advantage, because the discussion that follows tends to circle around it. A seller who opens high, within reason, usually settles higher than one who opens modestly.

Experts are not immune. In studies, experienced professionals asked to value a house or to fix a penalty have been swayed by figures they had been told were arbitrary. Knowing about the bias does not remove it, though it can weaken it.

The most practical defence is to set one's own anchor before hearing anyone else's. A buyer who has checked prices in three shops, or a borrower who has worked out what monthly instalment she can afford before visiting a lender, enters the conversation with a figure of her own. The other side's anchor still pulls, but now it pulls against something.

stimuli.title: The signature that binds
stimuli.content:
Few documents are signed as casually, or regretted as deeply, as a loan guarantee. A friend or relative needs a loan, the bank asks for a guarantor, and someone close to the borrower signs, often at the branch counter and often without reading the agreement. To the guarantor it feels like an act of friendship, a formality that costs nothing. It is, in fact, a promise to repay someone else's debt.

The promise is not a weak one. In India, as in many other countries, the law treats a guarantor's liability as co-extensive with that of the borrower. If the borrower defaults, the lender is generally free to demand the money from the guarantor without first suing the borrower or selling his property. Suppose a man borrows ₹5,00,000, repays ₹2,00,000 of the principal and then stops paying, leaving ₹30,000 of interest unpaid. The bank may ask his guarantor for ₹3,30,000, together with any further interest and charges it is entitled to recover.

The consequences reach beyond money. A default by the borrower can be reported against the guarantor as well, and a person who has guaranteed one large loan may find banks reluctant to lend to her, because part of her capacity to borrow is already spoken for. In this sense a guarantee is a latent debt: it does not appear in one's own accounts, but it can surface at any time.

Why, then, do so many people sign? Partly because refusing feels like an insult to the borrower. Partly because the risk seems remote: the borrower is a cousin with a steady job, or a friend whose business is doing well. Guarantees, however, are asked for precisely because lenders are not sure that the loan will be repaid.

None of this means that one should never stand guarantee. It means that a guarantee deserves the same scrutiny as a loan of one's own. A careful guarantor reads the agreement, asks how the borrower plans to repay, keeps track of whether instalments are being paid, and signs only for an amount she could afford to lose.

stimuli.title: Each generation's normal
stimuli.content:
Ask an elderly fisherman on almost any Indian coast about the sea of his youth, and he will describe catches that sound like exaggerations: nets so heavy that three men struggled to haul them in, fish as long as a man's arm, sharks seen close to the shore. Ask his grandson, who fishes the same waters today, and he will describe a good day that his grandfather would have called a poor one. Yet the grandson does not feel that anything has been lost. The sea he knows is the only sea he has known.

The fisheries scientist Daniel Pauly gave this pattern a name in the 1990s: the shifting baseline. Each generation, he argued, takes the state of the world it first encounters as normal, and measures decline only from that point. Losses that happened before its time are invisible to it. Over several generations, a resource can be reduced to a fraction of its former abundance without any single generation witnessing a dramatic collapse.

The idea reaches well beyond fishing. City dwellers who grew up under a hazy sky may regard a few clear days as unusually good rather than as what the sky once was. Birdwatchers who began counting a species when it was already scarce may record no fall at all. Even official targets can be affected: a plan to 'restore' a river to its condition of thirty years ago may aim at a state that was itself badly degraded.

The difficulty is partly one of evidence. Older conditions were seldom measured with the care that today's surveys demand, and memories, as critics rightly point out, can be selective or romantic. An old man's recollection of giant fish is not data. But dismissing such accounts altogether carries its own risk, since it leaves the most recent, and most depleted, state as the only one that counts.

Researchers have therefore turned to unconventional sources: old photographs of fishermen posing with their catch, market records, colonial gazetteers, even the menus of restaurants. None of these is precise, but together they can show the direction and rough size of a change that no living observer can see in full.

The lesson is not that the past was always better. It is that our sense of what is normal is borrowed from a short span of experience, and that a society which wishes to protect what remains must first find out what has already gone.

stimuli.title: A string with an edge
stimuli.content:
On festival days in many towns, the sky fills with kites, and on the rooftops below, children and adults battle to cut one another's strings. To win these contests, many fliers use a string coated with powdered glass. Such a string can (1) ______ through a rival's thread in seconds, and the winner's shout of triumph rings across the lanes.

The same sharpness makes it dangerous. Every season, thousands of birds, especially pigeons and black kites, fly into loose strings that hang from trees, poles and wires, and many of them die of their (2) ______. Strings stretched across roads have also cut the necks of people riding two-wheelers, sometimes fatally.

Several states have banned glass-coated string, and some cities have gone further, banning strings made of nylon and other synthetic materials, which do not snap easily. Yet the ban is hard to (3) ______. The string is cheap, it is sold quietly from small shops and homes, and demand rises sharply in the few days before the festival, when the police have many other duties.

Volunteers have stepped in where the law falls short. In some cities, groups set up bird-rescue camps where vets stitch the wounds of injured birds and release them once they have healed. Others go from roof to roof after the festival, collecting the tangled string that would otherwise (4) ______ hanging from trees and wires for months.

Many riders now fix a thin metal rod in front of the handlebar of their scooters, which catches any string before it reaches the rider's neck. Such rods help, but doctors and police (5) ______ that the safest solution is a simple one: fly kites with plain cotton thread, which breaks long before it can wound.

stimuli.title: The case for the roundabout
stimuli.content:
At a busy crossroads controlled by traffic lights, drivers spend much of their time waiting. Even when no vehicle is coming from any other direction, a red light holds them back until it (1) ______. A well-designed roundabout works differently. Vehicles entering it give way to the traffic already circling and then move on as soon as there is a gap, so that at quiet hours almost nobody has to stop at all.

Safety experts value roundabouts for a further reason. At an ordinary crossing, the most serious crashes are side-on or head-on collisions between vehicles moving at speed. A roundabout (2) ______ such crashes almost impossible: all traffic moves in one direction, and the curve forces drivers to slow down. Accidents still happen, but they tend to be minor scrapes rather than deadly impacts.

Roundabouts are not a cure for every junction, however. When traffic is very heavy on one road and light on the others, the busy stream may never leave a gap, and vehicles on the quieter roads can wait for a long time. Large roundabouts can also be hard for pedestrians and cyclists to (3) ______, since there is no pause in the flow of vehicles. In many cities, such circles have been fitted with traffic lights for the rush hours, which (4) ______ much of their advantage.

Much also depends on drivers. A roundabout works only if those entering it actually give way. Where drivers push in regardless, the circle quickly becomes a knot of vehicles, each blocking the next. Engineers therefore stress that good design must be (5) ______ by clear signs, road markings and the steady enforcement of one simple rule: give way to the traffic already on the circle.

stimuli.title: Holes that come back
stimuli.content:
Every monsoon, the roads of many Indian cities break out in potholes. They appear so **(1) regularly** that many residents treat them as a season of their own, like the rains that bring them. Yet potholes are not an act of nature. Engineers say that most of them can be traced to two causes: water and poor construction.

A road surface is meant to shed rain into the drains along its edges. When the surface is laid without the proper slope, or when the drains are **(2) cleared**, water stands on the road and slowly seeps into small cracks. Heavy vehicles passing over the weakened patch press the water down and force it out again, loosening the stones beneath. Within days a crack can **(3) shrink** into a hole deep enough to throw a rider off a scooter.

The usual response makes matters worse. Crews arrive after the rains, shovel loose material into the hole and press it down with a roller or even with their feet. Such patches are cheap and quick, but they rarely bond with the old surface, and the next heavy shower washes them out. The city then pays for the same hole again and again, a cycle that some critics believe is **(4) convenient** for contractors.

Better methods exist. A pothole can be cut into a neat rectangle, cleaned, dried and filled with material that is pressed down in thin layers, so that the repair **(5) crumbles** for years. Some cities also write a defect liability period into road contracts, under which the contractor must repair, at his own cost, any damage that appears within a fixed number of years. Where such clauses are **(6) ignored**, contractors have a reason to build well the first time.

Residents can help too. Several cities now allow people to photograph a pothole and report it through an app, and some publish how quickly each complaint is closed. Records of this kind make it harder for the same hole to be patched, forgotten and paid for, year after year.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, when is the danger of snakebite the greatest?

options.text: During the summer, when village wells run dry
During the winter, when farmers sleep indoors
During the monsoon, when rain floods the burrows of rats
During the harvest festival, when crowds gather

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The monsoon months, when rain floods the burrows of rats and drives out the snakes that hunt them, are the most dangerous.'
steps: It refers to the monsoon months
solution.why_others_wrong: Winter, summer and festivals are never mentioned as dangerous times; the passage names only the monsoon months.
solution.final_answer: Option C: During the monsoon, when rain floods the burrows of rats

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, when does antivenom work best?

options.text: When it is taken regularly before going to the fields
When it is given only after the limb has swollen
When it is given early, within a few hours of the bite
When it is mixed with herbs by a local healer

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: antivenom 'works best when it is given early, ideally within a few hours of the bite.'
steps: Given early, within a few hours
solution.why_others_wrong: Herbs are mentioned only as a healer's treatment that wastes time. Waiting for swelling contradicts 'given early'. Taking it before going to the fields is never suggested.
solution.final_answer: Option C: When it is given early, within a few hours of the bite

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT advised in the passage for a person who has been bitten by a snake?

options.text: Removing rings and bangles before the limb swells
Sucking the venom out of the wound
Being carried to a hospital as quickly as possible

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage advises
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 advises keeping the limb still, removing rings and bangles and carrying the victim to hospital. It says that trying to suck out the venom 'does no good'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping the limb still, removing rings and bangles and carrying the victim to hospital are all advised in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Sucking the venom out of the wound

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'Precious' as used in the passage ('Precious hours are lost')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: precious = of great value, not to be wasted
solution.explanation: Antivenom works best within a few hours, so every hour after a bite is of great value. Hours spent at a healer's are 'precious' hours lost: valuable time.
steps: Context: antivenom works best within a few hours
solution.why_others_wrong: The hours are badly needed, not 'needless', and 'peaceful' and 'ordinary' say nothing about their importance.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, should a snakebite victim be carried rather than made to walk?

options.text: Walking makes the victim reach the hospital too late at night.
Hospitals do not admit patients who arrive on foot.
Carrying the victim keeps the wound clean of mud.
Walking moves the limb, which helps the venom spread.

solution.concept: Inference: linking two pieces of advice in the same paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the bitten limb should be kept still 'because movement helps the venom spread'. Walking would move the limb, so the victim should be carried.
steps: Advice: keep the bitten limb still
solution.why_others_wrong: Time of night and hospital rules are never mentioned. Mud and clean wounds are not discussed; the reason given is that movement spreads the venom.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Walking moves the limb, which helps the venom spread.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage describes snakebite deaths, says most can be prevented, explains why victims reach hospital late, gives first-aid advice and ends with prevention. Its concern throughout is saving lives.
steps: Para 1: the scale of the problem
Paras 2-4: deaths are preventable; delays and advice
Para 5: prevention: 'the difference between life and death'
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage is about bites in farms and villages, not forest snakes. Healers appear in one paragraph only. How antivenom is made is never described.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Saving Lives After a Snakebite

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do local residents rarely notice that their homes lack a proper address?

options.text: They know their neighbourhood by heart.
Their town has already named all its streets.
They always travel with a local guide.
They seldom receive any letters or parcels.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Local residents rarely notice the problem, because they know their neighbourhood by heart.'
steps: They know the area by heart
solution.why_others_wrong: Receiving few letters and travelling with guides are never mentioned. If the streets were already named, there would be no problem to notice.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They know their neighbourhood by heart.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does a parcel that cannot be delivered affect customers?

options.text: They receive the parcel free of charge the next time.
They must collect it themselves from the nearest police station.
Part of the cost of returning and resending it is passed on to them.
They are fined by the delivery company for a wrong address.

solution.concept: Locating a stated consequence
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: the parcel 'must be carried back, stored and sent out again, and some of that cost is passed on to customers.'
steps: Costs: carried back, stored, sent again
Some cost is passed on to customers
solution.why_others_wrong: Collecting parcels from a police station, fines and free delivery are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Part of the cost of returning and resending it is passed on to them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'obvious' as used in the passage ('An ambulance driver is the most obvious example')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: obvious = easily seen or understood
solution.explanation: The ambulance driver is the example that comes to mind first and is easiest to see, because a delay can cost a life. 'Most obvious' means clearest.
steps: Context: delay costs a patient's life
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hidden' is the opposite of obvious. 'Unusual' and 'recent' do not describe how easy the example is to see.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as something that usually requires proof of where one lives?

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists opening a bank account, getting a gas connection and applying for a loan. Booking a bus ticket is never mentioned.
steps: Bus ticket: not in the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: The bank account, the gas connection and the loan are all named in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Booking a bus ticket

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the passage suggest is the main limitation of the digital location codes?

options.text: They are too long for most people to write on an envelope.
They are useful only if residents know their codes and services can read them.
They depend entirely on the knowledge of local shopkeepers.
They cannot describe places where streets have no names.

solution.concept: Inference: a limitation stated with 'but'
solution.explanation: Paragraph 5: the codes 'do not depend on local knowledge, but they work only if people know their own code and the services that need it can read it.' The condition after 'but' is their limitation.
steps: Strength: no need for local knowledge
Residents and services must both use the code
solution.why_others_wrong: The codes work 'even where there are no street names' and 'do not depend on local knowledge', so two options contradict the passage. The codes are called 'a short string', so length is not a problem.
solution.final_answer: Option B: They are useful only if residents know their codes and services can read them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by the closing words 'It is a way of being found'?

options.text: An address helps lost travellers find their way back home.
An address allows the police to track people who move often.
An address lets services and institutions reach and recognise a person.
An address shows how long a family has lived in a town.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a summing-up sentence
solution.explanation: The passage shows that without an address, ambulances, fire engines and deliveries cannot find a home, and families cannot prove where they live to banks or gas agencies. Being 'found' means being reached and recognised by such services.
steps: All need to locate or recognise a home
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage is about others finding a home, not travellers finding their way. An address does not show how long a family has lived somewhere (paragraph 4 makes the opposite point). Tracking people is never discussed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: An address lets services and institutions reach and recognise a person.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do the phone-number experiments described in the passage show?

options.text: An unrelated number can influence how much people are willing to pay.
People refuse to state a price when they are unsure of an item's value.
People with high phone numbers usually have more money to spend.
Most buyers can judge the true value of an ordinary item easily.

solution.concept: Inference: the point an example is meant to prove
solution.explanation: The digits 'have nothing to do with the item', yet people with high digits offer more. A number that 'should carry no weight' pulls their judgement towards itself.
steps: The digits are irrelevant to the item
An irrelevant number sways the price people offer
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage never links phone numbers to wealth; the digits are random. If buyers could judge value easily, the digits would not sway them. People do state prices in the experiment.
solution.final_answer: Option A: An unrelated number can influence how much people are willing to pay.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the sari example, the discount (the marked price minus the sale price) is what percentage of the marked price of ₹6,000?

solution.concept: Percentage reduction = (marked price − sale price) ÷ marked price × 100
solution.explanation: The reduction is ₹6,000 − ₹4,500 = ₹1,500. As a share of the marked price: 1,500 ÷ 6,000 × 100 = 25%.
solution.shortcut: 1,500 is one quarter of 6,000, so the cut is 25%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 33% divides the reduction by the sale price instead of the marked price. 20% has no basis in the figures. 75% is the sale price as a share of the marked price, not the discount.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'arbitrary' as used in the passage ('figures they had been told were arbitrary')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: arbitrary = based on chance or whim, not on reason
solution.explanation: The point of the studies is that the figures had no real basis, yet they still swayed experts. 'Arbitrary' figures are ones chosen at random.
steps: Context: figures that should not matter
solution.why_others_wrong: If the figures were 'carefully calculated' or 'officially approved', being swayed by them would not show a bias. 'Widely published' says nothing about whether they had any basis.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why does a seller who opens high usually settle at a higher price?

options.text: A high opening figure shows that the seller has many other buyers.
Buyers trust sellers who ask for more than the item is worth.
The bargaining that follows tends to stay close to the first figure named.
Buyers are not allowed to name a figure of their own.

solution.concept: Inference: applying the idea of an anchor to bargaining
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: the side that names the first figure gains, 'because the discussion that follows tends to circle around it.' A high first figure keeps the final price high.
solution.why_others_wrong: Trust, other buyers and rules against buyers' figures are never mentioned. In fact, paragraph 5 advises buyers to bring a figure of their own.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The bargaining that follows tends to stay close to the first figure named.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: With which of the following statements would the author most probably agree?

options.text: Preparing a figure of one's own weakens, but does not cancel, the pull of an anchor.
Buyers should always let the seller name the first price.
Experts are completely protected from anchoring by their long experience.
Once people learn about anchoring, it no longer affects their judgement.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's position, drawn from the last two paragraphs
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: knowing about the bias 'does not remove it, though it can weaken it.' Paragraph 5: with a figure of one's own, the other side's anchor 'still pulls, but now it pulls against something.'
steps: Para 4: the bias can be weakened, not removed
Para 5: one's own figure resists the pull
The pull remains, but it is reduced
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Experts are not immune', so they are not completely protected. Knowing about the bias 'does not remove it'. Letting the seller go first would hand him the anchor, the opposite of the author's advice.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Preparing a figure of one's own weakens, but does not cancel, the pull of an anchor.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: The Pull of the First Number

solution.concept: Title: the central idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: Every paragraph is about how a first figure pulls later judgements towards it: in experiments, in shops, in negotiations, among experts, and how to resist it.
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage suggests discounts can mislead, not that they are always genuine. House valuation is one example in one sentence. Phone numbers are a random input, not a measure of wealth.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The Pull of the First Number

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what may a lender generally do if the borrower defaults?

options.text: Recover from the guarantor only the interest, not the principal.
Demand the money from the guarantor without first suing the borrower.
Approach the guarantor only after selling all of the borrower's property.
Cancel the guarantee and write off the whole of the loan.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'the lender is generally free to demand the money from the guarantor without first suing the borrower or selling his property.'
steps: Find 'If the borrower defaults' in paragraph 2
Lender may go straight to the guarantor
No need to sue the borrower first
solution.why_others_wrong: Selling the borrower's property first is exactly what the lender need not do. The example makes the guarantor liable for principal and interest. Writing off the loan is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Demand the money from the guarantor without first suing the borrower.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the example in paragraph 2, if no further interest or charges are added, how much can the bank ask the guarantor to pay?

solution.concept: Guarantor's liability = unpaid principal + unpaid interest (co-extensive with the borrower's)
solution.explanation: Unpaid principal = ₹5,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Adding the unpaid interest of ₹30,000 gives ₹3,30,000, the figure the passage states.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,00,000 leaves out the unpaid interest. ₹5,30,000 ignores the ₹2,00,000 already repaid. ₹2,30,000 adds the repaid amount instead of the unpaid one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author imply by saying that part of a guarantor's 'capacity to borrow is already spoken for'?

options.text: The borrower has the right to use her savings without asking her.
She has already borrowed money from the same bank for her own needs.
She has promised in writing never to take out a loan of her own.
Lenders treat the guarantee as a possible claim on her ability to repay her own loans.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a figurative phrase in its context
solution.explanation: The sentence explains why banks are reluctant to lend to a guarantor. Since she may have to pay the guaranteed loan, banks count part of her repaying ability as already committed. The next sentence calls the guarantee 'a latent debt'.
steps: Context: banks reluctant to lend to a guarantor
Reason: she may have to pay the guaranteed loan
Part of her repaying ability is already committed
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing says she has borrowed for herself or promised never to borrow. The borrower gets no right to her savings; the risk is that the lender may claim from her.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Lenders treat the guarantee as a possible claim on her ability to repay her own loans.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'latent' as used in the passage ('a guarantee is a latent debt')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: latent = existing but hidden or not yet active
solution.explanation: The passage explains the word itself: the guarantee 'does not appear in one's own accounts, but it can surface at any time.' It is a debt that exists but is not yet visible.
steps: Gloss after the colon: does not appear ... can surface
solution.why_others_wrong: A debt that can 'surface at any time' is not 'already fully repaid', and one that 'does not appear' is not 'openly acknowledged'. The passage stresses that the guarantee is binding, not 'legally invalid'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: present but not yet visible

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards standing guarantee for a loan?

options.text: Cautionary: it is not forbidden, but it should be weighed like one's own loan.
Indifferent: the risks are too small to deserve any real attention.
Approving: it is a harmless act of friendship that costs nothing at all.
Hostile: no sensible person should ever sign a guarantee for anyone.

solution.concept: Tone: read the conclusion, where the author states a position
solution.explanation: The final paragraph says: 'None of this means that one should never stand guarantee. It means that a guarantee deserves the same scrutiny as a loan of one's own.' This is a warning, not a ban.
steps: Paras 1-4: the hidden risks of guaranteeing
solution.why_others_wrong: The author calls the 'costs nothing' view a mistake, so the attitude is not approving. 'None of this means that one should never stand guarantee' rules out hostility. Spending a whole passage on the risks rules out indifference.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Cautionary: it is not forbidden, but it should be weighed like one's own loan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, does the young fisherman not feel that anything has been lost?

options.text: He does not believe his grandfather's stories about the past.
His catches are in fact larger than his grandfather's ever were.
He judges the sea by the state in which he first came to know it.
He has moved to waters that were never fished in the past.

solution.concept: Inference: applying the 'shifting baseline' to the opening example
solution.explanation: 'The sea he knows is the only sea he has known.' Paragraph 2 explains: each generation 'takes the state of the world it first encounters as normal'. The grandson's normal is already a depleted sea.
steps: Para 1: the grandson's good day = the grandfather's poor day
Para 2: each generation's first view = normal
So the loss is invisible to him
solution.why_others_wrong: His catches are smaller, not larger. The passage never says he disbelieves his grandfather; the point is that he has no memory of the earlier sea. He fishes 'the same waters'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He judges the sea by the state in which he first came to know it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the example of the plan to 'restore' a river (paragraph 3) illustrate?

options.text: Thirty years is long enough to measure any change in the natural world.
Rivers recover faster than fisheries once pollution has been stopped.
Official plans are usually based on very old and accurate records.
Targets for recovery may themselves be set from an already degraded state.

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of an example
solution.explanation: The plan aims at the river's condition thirty years ago, but that condition 'was itself badly degraded'. The target is fixed from a baseline that had already shifted.
steps: Restore to: the state of thirty years ago
The baseline problem affects official targets too
solution.why_others_wrong: The speed of recovery is not discussed, and the passage says older conditions were 'seldom measured with the care' surveys now demand, so old records are not called accurate. The example suggests thirty years is too short a window, not long enough.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Targets for recovery may themselves be set from an already degraded state.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's view of the old fishermen's memories?

options.text: They are the only evidence of past conditions that survives.
They are more reliable than any modern scientific survey.
They are exaggerations that researchers should simply ignore.
They are not data, but they should be weighed rather than dismissed.

solution.concept: Inference: a balanced position stated with 'But'
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 concedes that 'An old man's recollection of giant fish is not data', but warns that 'dismissing such accounts altogether carries its own risk'. The author wants them treated with care, not thrown out.
steps: Concession: memories can be selective, not data
Position: weigh them, do not ignore them
solution.why_others_wrong: The author warns against ignoring them and does not rank them above surveys. Paragraph 5 lists other sources (photographs, market records, gazetteers, menus), so they are not the only evidence.
solution.final_answer: Option D: They are not data, but they should be weighed rather than dismissed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'depleted' as used in the passage ('the most recent, and most depleted, state')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: depleted = reduced in quantity, used up
solution.explanation: The passage describes a resource reduced generation after generation, so the most recent state is the one with the least left: the most depleted, or most greatly reduced.
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing in the passage suggests the latest state is restored or admired. 'Carefully recorded' is about measurement, while the word describes how much of the resource is left.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: The Golden Age of Indian Fisheries

solution.concept: Title: the central idea, not one example or a claim the author rejects
solution.explanation: The passage explains how each generation's idea of 'normal' shifts downward, hiding long-term losses, and how researchers try to recover older baselines.
steps: Conclusion: our sense of normal comes from a short span
solution.why_others_wrong: The author does not say the fishermen exaggerate, and says 'The lesson is not that the past was always better', which rules out a golden-age title. Surveys have not replaced memory; the author wants both, plus other sources.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Normal That Keeps Moving

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what a sharp string does to another thread
solution.explanation: A glass-coated string is sharp and is used to cut a rival's thread quickly. A sharp edge 'slices through' a thread.
steps: Purpose: to cut one another's strings
solution.why_others_wrong: Strings do not 'melt', 'wander' or 'float' through a thread, and none of these would let the flier win by cutting.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the cause of death after being caught in a sharp string
solution.explanation: The paragraph is about the danger of the sharp string. Birds caught in it are cut and many 'die of their injuries'.
steps: Topic: 'The same sharpness makes it dangerous'
Birds are cut by the string
solution.why_others_wrong: Birds do not die of their 'songs', 'nests' or 'colours'; none of these is caused by a sharp string.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the sentences after 'Yet' explain the difficulty
solution.explanation: The string is cheap, sold quietly and in high demand while the police are busy. These are reasons why a ban is hard to put into effect: hard to 'enforce'.
steps: Reasons: cheap, sold quietly, police busy
Hard to make the ban work → 'enforce'
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing about the cheap, quietly sold string makes a ban hard to 'admire', 'describe' or 'repeat'; the reasons listed are all about making the ban work.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what uncollected string would do
solution.explanation: Volunteers collect the string because otherwise it would stay where it is: it would 'remain hanging from trees and wires for months'.
solution.why_others_wrong: If the string would 'vanish', there would be no need to collect it. 'Travel hanging' and 'shrink hanging' make no sense with 'for months'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: experts stating a firm opinion
solution.explanation: Doctors and police strongly hold the view that cotton thread is the safest solution. They 'insist that' it is so.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Deny that the safest solution is ...' would reject the advice that the sentence goes on to give. 'Forget' and 'regret' do not fit people recommending a solution.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what releases drivers waiting at a red light
solution.explanation: Drivers wait at a red light even when the road is empty; they can move only when the light turns green, that is, when it 'changes'.
steps: 'a red light holds them back until it ___'
Drivers go when the light turns green
solution.why_others_wrong: A light that 'dims' or 'glows' is still red. A light that 'fails' is a fault, not the normal event drivers wait for.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: verb + object + adjective ('make something impossible')
solution.explanation: The pattern 'make + object + adjective' means cause it to become so: a roundabout 'makes such crashes almost impossible', because all traffic moves one way.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Takes', 'gives' and 'holds' are not used with an object followed by an adjective to mean 'cause to become'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the reason clause decides the word
solution.explanation: 'Since there is no pause in the flow of vehicles', people on foot or on cycles find large roundabouts hard to get across: hard to 'cross'.
steps: Reason: no pause in the flow of vehicles
A continuous flow blocks those trying to get across
solution.why_others_wrong: A continuous flow of vehicles does not make a roundabout hard to 'see', 'clean' or 'light'; it makes it hard to cross.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the effect of adding traffic lights to a roundabout
solution.explanation: The roundabout's advantage is that vehicles need not wait for a light. Fitting lights brings the waiting back, which 'cancels much of their advantage'.
steps: Advantage of a roundabout: no waiting at lights
solution.why_others_wrong: Adding lights does not 'double' the advantage; it removes it. 'Explains' and 'reveals' do not fit an action that takes something away.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: design needs help from signs and enforcement
solution.explanation: The paragraph says a roundabout works only if drivers give way, so design alone is not enough. It must be 'supported by' signs, markings and enforcement.
steps: Design alone fails if drivers push in
Signs and enforcement add to the design
solution.why_others_wrong: Engineers would not want good design 'replaced', 'delayed' or 'hidden'; the signs and enforcement are meant to work along with it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'They appear so regularly that many residents treat them as a season of their own'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'so ... that' result must match the cause
solution.explanation: People treat potholes 'as a season of their own' because they come back every monsoon, i.e. they appear regularly. 'Regularly' fits.
steps: A season comes back every year
solution.why_others_wrong: If potholes appeared 'rarely', no one would treat them as a season. 'Quietly' and 'cheaply' do not explain the comparison with a season.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'when the surface is laid without the proper slope, or when the drains are cleared, water stands on the road'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: cause and effect must agree
solution.explanation: Water stands on the road when it cannot run off into the drains. Cleared drains would carry water away; drains that are 'blocked' make it stand.
steps: Effect: water stands on the road
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Repaired' drains would work better, not cause standing water. 'Numbered' has nothing to do with drainage. 'Cleared' gives the opposite cause, so the word must be replaced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'Within days a crack can shrink into a hole deep enough to throw a rider off a scooter'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a small crack becoming a deep hole
solution.explanation: A small crack that turns into a deep hole grows larger; it does not get smaller. The verb must be 'widen into'.
steps: End: hole deep enough to throw a rider
solution.why_others_wrong: A crack does not 'harden' or 'dry' into a deep hole; neither describes growth. 'Shrink' contradicts the change from crack to hole.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'The city then pays for the same hole again and again, a cycle that some critics believe is convenient for contractors'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: read the critics' suspicion from the context
solution.explanation: Each time a patch washes out, the city pays again, and contractors earn again. Critics suspect the cycle suits contractors: it is 'convenient' for them. The word fits.
steps: The cycle suits them → 'convenient' is correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The city, not the contractor, bears the cost, so 'costly' and 'harmful' for contractors miss the critics' point. 'Unknown' makes no sense of a cycle the critics have noticed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'filled with material that is pressed down in thin layers, so that the repair crumbles for years'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the purpose of a better method
solution.explanation: The paragraph describes 'better methods'. Their purpose is a repair that holds 'for years': one that 'lasts'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A repair that 'sinks' or 'bends' for years is a failed repair, not the aim of a better method. 'Crumbles' is the opposite of the purpose, so it must be replaced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (6) may be wrongly used: 'Where such clauses are ignored, contractors have a reason to build well the first time'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a contract clause gives an incentive only if it is applied
solution.explanation: A contractor who must repair damage at his own cost has a reason to build well, but only where the clause is actually applied, i.e. 'enforced'.
steps: Clause: contractor pays for later damage
Incentive works only if the clause is applied
solution.why_others_wrong: Clauses that are 'forgotten' or 'hidden' give no incentive, just like ignored ones. 'Ignored' contradicts the result 'have a reason to build well'.

questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Sunil is best player (A) / in our office (B) / cricket team. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: A superlative adjective before a noun takes 'the'
solution.explanation: 'Best' is a superlative and picks out one player from the team, so it needs 'the': 'Sunil is the best player in our office cricket team.'
steps: 'is best player' → 'is the best player': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct place phrase. Part C correctly completes the noun phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Sunil is best player

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
When I was six, (A) / my grandfather learnt me (B) / how to ride a bicycle. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Learn = gain knowledge yourself; teach = give knowledge to someone else
solution.explanation: The grandfather gave the skill to the child, so the verb is 'teach': 'my grandfather taught me how to ride a bicycle.' One learns from someone; one teaches someone.
steps: Who gives the skill? The grandfather
'learnt me' → 'taught me': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time clause. Part C ('how to ride a bicycle') correctly follows 'taught me'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: my grandfather learnt me

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
After the long meeting, (A) / all the members went (B) / to home early. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Home' after verbs of motion (go, come, return) takes no preposition
solution.explanation: 'Home' here works as an adverb of place, so no 'to' is used: 'all the members went home early.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part B has a correct subject and past tense. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Ravi, who lives next door, (A) / teaches mathematics (B) / at a college in the town. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: at a college in the town.

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: check the relative clause, agreement and prepositions
solution.explanation: 'Who lives next door' correctly describes Ravi and is set off by commas. 'Ravi ... teaches' is singular and agrees. 'Mathematics' is the subject taught, and 'at a college in the town' is correct.
steps: 'at a college in the town': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: No part contains an error: the relative clause, the verb and the place phrase are all correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The train from Delhi (A) / arrived lately (B) / because of the thick fog. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Late (adverb) = after the expected time; lately = recently
solution.explanation: The train came after its expected time, which is 'late': 'The train from Delhi arrived late because of the thick fog.' 'Lately' means 'recently', as in 'I have not seen him lately.'
steps: 'arrived lately' → 'arrived late': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part C correctly gives the reason. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Most people in this town (A) / feel that the new mall (B) / is too much expensive. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Too' + adjective is strengthened by 'much' placed before it: 'much too expensive', never 'too much expensive'
solution.explanation: 'Too much' is used before nouns ('too much noise'). Before an adjective, the intensifier comes first: 'is much too expensive'.
steps: 'too much expensive' → 'much too expensive': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject phrase. Part B correctly introduces the clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: is too much expensive.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Before he moved to the village, (A) / the old man divided his savings (B) / equally among his two sons. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Before he moved to the village,
the old man divided his savings

solution.concept: 'Between' is used for two people or things; 'among' for more than two
solution.explanation: There are only two sons, so the savings are divided 'between' them: 'equally between his two sons.'
steps: Two → between; more than two → among
'among his two sons' → 'between his two sons': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time clause. Part B is a correct main clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: equally among his two sons.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The flood victims were deprived from (A) / food and clean water (B) / for nearly three days. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The flood victims were deprived from

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: deprive someone of something
solution.explanation: The verb 'deprive' takes 'of': 'The flood victims were deprived of food and clean water for nearly three days.'
steps: 'deprived from' → 'deprived of': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct object. Part C is a correct duration phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The flood victims were deprived from

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new water filter consists from (A) / three layers of sand, (B) / gravel and charcoal. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The new water filter consists from

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: consist of (be made up of)
solution.explanation: 'Consist' takes 'of' when it lists parts: 'The new water filter consists of three layers of sand, gravel and charcoal.'
steps: 'consists from' → 'consists of': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B and part C correctly list the materials. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The new water filter consists from

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The courier could not lift (A) / the parcel alone (B) / because it was such heavy. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'So' goes before an adjective alone; 'such' goes before a noun phrase (such a heavy parcel)
solution.explanation: 'Heavy' is an adjective with no noun after it, so the intensifier is 'so': 'because it was so heavy.' 'Such' would need a noun: 'such a heavy parcel'.
steps: After 'such': a noun phrase is needed
'such heavy' → 'so heavy': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A has a correct modal and verb. Part B is a correct object and adverb. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: because it was such heavy.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Members are requested (A) / to refrain to smoke (B) / inside the reading room. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: refrain from + -ing
solution.explanation: 'Refrain' is followed by 'from' and a gerund: 'Members are requested to refrain from smoking inside the reading room.'
steps: 'to refrain to smoke' → 'to refrain from smoking': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct passive request. Part C is a correct place phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to refrain to smoke

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Whether he comes or not, (A) / the meeting will begin (B) / at ten sharp. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: 'whether ... or not' clause + future in the main clause
solution.explanation: 'Whether he comes or not' is a correct concessive clause, with the present tense for a future event. 'The meeting will begin at ten sharp' is a correct main clause.
steps: Present 'comes' in the subordinate clause, future 'will begin' in the main clause
solution.why_others_wrong: No part has an error: the clause, the tenses and the time phrase are all correct.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The leaking roof of the warehouse (A) / needs to repair (B) / before the monsoon arrives. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The leaking roof of the warehouse

solution.concept: When the subject receives the action, 'need' takes a passive infinitive (needs to be repaired) or a gerund (needs repairing)
solution.explanation: The roof cannot repair anything; it is to be repaired. So the infinitive must be passive: 'needs to be repaired' (or 'needs repairing').
steps: 'needs to repair' → 'needs to be repaired': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject. Part C correctly uses the present tense in a time clause about the future. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Having found cheaper software, (A) / the firm decided (B) / to dispense of its old accountant's services. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: to dispense of its old accountant's services.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: dispense with = do without, get rid of
solution.explanation: To stop using someone's services is to 'dispense with' them: 'the firm decided to dispense with its old accountant's services.'
steps: 'dispense of' → 'dispense with': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct participle phrase whose subject is the firm. Part B is a correct main clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to dispense of its old accountant's services.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The old farmer refused to part from (A) / the wooden plough (B) / that his father had made for him. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The old farmer refused to part from
that his father had made for him.

solution.concept: Part with = give up possession of a thing; part from = leave a person
solution.explanation: A plough is a thing he refuses to give up, so the phrase is 'part with': 'The old farmer refused to part with the wooden plough ...'. 'Part from' is used for leaving a person ('parted from his friends').
steps: Give up a thing → part with
'part from' → 'part with': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct object. Part C correctly uses the past perfect for the earlier action. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The old farmer refused to part from

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
He is an alumni (A) / of the same college (B) / where his father studied. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Alumnus (one person) / alumni (plural)
solution.explanation: 'Alumni' is the plural of 'alumnus'. One person is 'an alumnus': 'He is an alumnus of the same college where his father studied.'
steps: 'an alumni' → 'an alumnus': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct prepositional phrase. Part C is a correct relative clause. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He is an alumni

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Watching the old craftsman at work, (A) / we could not but to admire (B) / the patience in his hands. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Watching the old craftsman at work,
we could not but to admire

solution.concept: 'Cannot but' (= cannot help) is followed by the bare infinitive, without 'to'
solution.explanation: 'Cannot but' means 'cannot do anything except', and takes the bare infinitive: 'we could not but admire the patience in his hands.'
steps: 'not but to admire' → 'not but admire': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct participle phrase with 'we' as its subject. Part C is a correct object. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: we could not but to admire

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
I have yet to receive (A) / a reply from the head office (B) / about my transfer request. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: a reply from the head office

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: 'have yet to + verb' = have not done so far
solution.explanation: 'I have yet to receive a reply' correctly means 'I have not received a reply so far'. 'From the head office' and 'about my transfer request' are correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: No part has an error. 'Have yet to' may look odd, but it is standard English.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Barely a month after it opened, (A) / the new branch had signed up (B) / over a thousand customers. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Barely a month after it opened,
the new branch had signed up

solution.concept: Error-free sentence: past perfect for a result reached by a past point in time
solution.explanation: 'Barely a month after it opened' fixes a past point. By then the branch 'had signed up' over a thousand customers: the past perfect is correct. 'Over a thousand customers' is a correct plural object.
steps: Past reference point: a month after opening
Result completed by then: past perfect
solution.why_others_wrong: No part has an error: 'barely' does not need inversion here because it modifies the time phrase, not the verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Each students** of the class must bring a photograph for the identity card.

solution.concept: 'Each' and 'every' are followed by a singular noun
solution.explanation: 'Each' refers to members one at a time and takes a singular noun: 'Each student of the class must bring a photograph ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Each of student' needs 'the' and a plural (each of the students). 'Every students' repeats the same mistake. The original uses a plural noun, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
It is getting dark; please **open the light** in the corridor.

solution.concept: Lights and fans are switched (or turned) on and off, not opened
solution.explanation: 'Open' is used for doors, windows and boxes. A light is 'switched on': 'please switch on the light in the corridor.'
steps: Verb for lights: switch on / turn on
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Open on the light' and 'start the light' are not used in English. 'Open the light' is a common error, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: switch on the light

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The other boys **were laughing on him** because he had fallen into the puddle.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: laugh at (someone) = mock or find funny
solution.explanation: To make fun of someone is to 'laugh at' him: 'The other boys were laughing at him because he had fallen into the puddle.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Laughing to him' and 'laughing over him' are not idiomatic for mocking someone. 'Laughing on him' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: were laughing at him

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Because the chief guest was unwell, the annual function was **postponed for next week**.

solution.concept: Postpone something to (or until) a later time
solution.explanation: When an event is moved to a later date, it is 'postponed to' that date: 'the annual function was postponed to next week.'
steps: The new time is introduced by 'to' (or 'until')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Postponed in next week' and 'postponed by next week' do not name the new date correctly ('by' would give the length of a delay, as in 'postponed by a week'). 'Postponed for next week' is not idiomatic, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: postponed to next week

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Nobody in the office knows **the reason of his sudden resignation**.

options.text: the reason about his sudden resignation
the reason for his sudden resignation
the reason to his sudden resignation

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: reason for (something)
solution.explanation: The noun 'reason' takes 'for': 'Nobody in the office knows the reason for his sudden resignation.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Reason about' and 'reason to' are not used with a noun in this sense. 'Reason of' is wrong, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: the reason for his sudden resignation

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
You **ought to inform** me yesterday that the branch would be closed today.

solution.concept: 'Ought to have + past participle' = a past duty that was not carried out
solution.explanation: The duty belonged to yesterday and was not done (the speaker was not told). A past unfulfilled duty is expressed by 'ought to have + past participle': 'You ought to have informed me yesterday ...'.
steps: The duty was not carried out
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ought to be informing' refers to the present or future and clashes with 'yesterday'. 'Ought to informed' puts a past form after 'to'. 'Ought to inform' cannot refer to yesterday, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: ought to have informed

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**What with the rain and the traffic**, we reached the station only a minute before the train left.

options.text: Because with the rain and the traffic
What for the rain and the traffic
Due with the rain and the traffic

solution.concept: 'What with A and B' = because of A and B (usually several troublesome causes)
solution.explanation: 'What with the rain and the traffic' is a correct idiom giving two reasons for the late arrival. The sentence is correct as it stands.
steps: Idiom: what with X and Y = because of X and Y
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Because with', 'What for' and 'Due with' are not English expressions. The bold part is a correct idiom, so no change is needed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Please **fill on** this form in capital letters and sign it at the bottom.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: fill in (a form) = write the required details in it
solution.explanation: Writing details into a form is 'filling it in': 'Please fill in this form in capital letters ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fill at' and 'fill by' are not phrasal verbs. 'Fill on' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The unsafe old building was **pulled up** last year, and a park now stands in its place.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: pull down (a building) = demolish it
solution.explanation: A building that is removed so that a park can take its place is demolished, i.e. 'pulled down'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Pull over' is what a vehicle does to stop at the side of a road. 'Pull through' means recover from an illness. 'Pull up' means stop a vehicle or remove a plant; none means demolish, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The thief **made off by** the cash box while the shopkeeper was busy with a customer.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: make off with (something) = steal it and run away
solution.explanation: A thief who runs away with stolen goods 'makes off with' them: 'The thief made off with the cash box ...'.
steps: Meaning: escaped carrying the cash box
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Made up with' means became friends again after a quarrel. 'Made out of' describes material. 'Made off by' is not idiomatic, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Worried about panic, the minister tried to **play up** the crisis, calling it a minor issue that would soon pass.

solution.concept: Play down = make something seem less important; play up = make it seem more important
solution.explanation: Calling the crisis 'a minor issue' makes it seem smaller, which is 'playing it down'. 'Play up' would mean exaggerating it, the opposite of what the minister did.
steps: Making something seem smaller = play down
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Play along' means pretend to agree. 'Play out' means happen or unfold. 'Play up' gives the opposite meaning, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: Please wait me at the school gate.
Please wait at me at the school gate.
Please wait for me at the school gate.
Please wait to me at the school gate.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: wait for (someone or something)
solution.explanation: The verb 'wait' takes 'for' before the person or thing waited for: 'Please wait for me at the school gate.'
solution.why_others_wrong: The other sentences drop the preposition or use 'to' or 'at', none of which is used with 'wait' in this sense.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Please wait for me at the school gate.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: He did nothing but complained about the food all evening.
There was nothing to do but sit and wait.
She could do nothing but wait for the next bus.
All he did was complain about the food.

solution.concept: 'Do nothing but' is followed by the bare infinitive
solution.explanation: After 'did nothing but', the verb takes its base form: 'He did nothing but complain about the food all evening.' 'Complained' is wrong.
steps: Pattern: do nothing but + base verb
