solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are correct: 'could do nothing but wait' and 'nothing to do but sit' use the base form, and 'All he did was complain' also takes the base form after 'did ... was'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He did nothing but complained about the food all evening.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) On his last day, he found the whole village waiting for him outside the post office.
(B) For thirty-two years, Hariram had delivered letters on foot to the scattered hamlets around Sonpur.
(C) In all that time, he had not missed a single day, not even during the great flood.
(D) Young men and women to whom he had once brought their exam results now handed him a garland and a new bicycle.
(E) When the news came that he was to retire, people began to realise how much they would miss him.

solution.concept: Para jumble: introduction → 'all that time' → news of retirement → last day → farewell gift
solution.explanation: B introduces Hariram and his thirty-two years. C ('In all that time') refers back to those years. E brings the news of his retirement. A describes his last day, and D the gift the villagers gave him that day.
steps: Opener: B (who he is, how long he served)
B → C: 'all that time' = the thirty-two years
E → A (last day) → D (the gift): BCEAD
solution.why_others_wrong: CBEAD opens with 'In all that time', which has nothing to refer to. BCADE puts the news of his retirement after his last day. BCEDA has the gift handed over before the village gathers on his last day.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) When a highway bypass is built around a small town, the town's shopkeepers often protest.
(P) Yet some towns find that, once the heavy lorries are gone, their markets become pleasanter places to shop, and local customers return.
(Q) Once the bypass opens, these vehicles no longer pass through the town at all.
(R) Their fear is easy to understand.
(S) Many of their customers are travellers whose buses, cars and lorries stop on the main road for tea, food or fuel.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'their fear' → reason → consequence → 'Yet' contrast
solution.explanation: R ('Their fear') refers to the protest in (1). S explains the fear: many customers are passing travellers. Q ('these vehicles') shows they will stop coming. P ('Yet') gives the surprising other side.
steps: Q → P: 'Yet' the unexpected benefit: RSQP
solution.why_others_wrong: RQSP puts 'these vehicles' before any vehicles are mentioned. SRQP separates 'Their fear' from the protest it refers to. RSPQ gives the 'Yet' contrast before the loss of travellers it contrasts with.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) When an onion is cut, its damaged cells release substances that mix and form an irritating gas.
(B) Anyone who has chopped onions knows that the job can bring tears to the eyes.
(C) The eyes respond by producing tears to wash the irritant away.
(D) This gas drifts upward and, on reaching the eyes, stings them.
(E) Chilling an onion before cutting it slows this process, which is why some cooks keep onions in the refrigerator.

solution.concept: Para jumble: common experience → cause → spread → body's response → practical tip
solution.explanation: B states the familiar experience. A explains what happens when the onion is cut. D ('This gas') follows the gas to the eyes. C gives the eyes' response. E offers a remedy based on the process.
steps: B → A: cutting releases a gas
A → D: 'This gas' reaches the eyes
D → C: tears → E: the remedy: BADCE
solution.why_others_wrong: BDACE uses 'This gas' before any gas is mentioned. ABDCE puts the general experience in the middle of the explanation. BADEC gives the remedy before explaining that the eyes water.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) A fixed deposit can usually be closed before it matures.
(P) A depositor who may need money at short notice can therefore split her savings into several smaller deposits.
(Q) Doing so, however, comes at a price.
(R) That way, she can break only one of them in an emergency and let the others earn their full interest.
(S) The bank usually pays a lower rate on the money withdrawn early, and may also charge a small penalty.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'Doing so' → the cost → 'therefore' → 'That way'
solution.explanation: Q ('Doing so') refers to closing the deposit early. S describes the price: a lower rate and a penalty. P ('therefore') gives the sensible response. R ('That way') explains how splitting helps.
solution.why_others_wrong: QPSR gives the advice before the cost that makes it necessary. SQPR describes the price before 'Doing so ... comes at a price' introduces it. QSRP uses 'That way' and 'them' before the smaller deposits are mentioned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) To correct this, an extra day, 29 February, is added to the calendar every fourth year.
(B) The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go once round the Sun.
(C) Without this adjustment, the seasons would slowly drift away from their usual months.
(D) Over four years, this shortfall adds up to roughly one whole day.
(E) A calendar of exactly 365 days therefore falls behind by about a quarter of a day each year.

solution.concept: Para jumble: fact → consequence → accumulation → correction → why it matters
solution.explanation: B gives the length of the Earth's year. E ('therefore') shows a 365-day calendar falls behind. D ('this shortfall') adds it up over four years. A ('To correct this') adds the leap day. C ('this adjustment') says what would happen without it.
steps: B → E: 'therefore' the calendar falls behind
D → A: the correction → C: 'Without this adjustment': BEDAC
solution.why_others_wrong: BDEAC uses 'this shortfall' before the shortfall is described. EBDAC opens with 'therefore', which needs a fact before it. BEDCA mentions 'this adjustment' before the adjustment is introduced.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Mohan had saved for two years to buy a second-hand bicycle.
(P) When he came out with a box of sweets for his mother, the bicycle was gone.
(Q) Two days later, a constable knocked at his door with the bicycle, which had been found abandoned near the railway station.
(R) On the very first day, he rode it to the market and parked it outside a sweet shop.
(S) He searched the nearby lanes until dark and then reported the theft at the police station.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; narrative order: ride → theft → search and report → recovery
solution.explanation: R: on the first day he parks the bicycle outside a sweet shop. P: he comes out to find it gone. S: he searches and reports the theft. Q: two days later the police return it.
steps: R → P: the bicycle is gone
S → Q: 'Two days later' it is returned: RPSQ
solution.why_others_wrong: RSPQ reports a theft before the bicycle is missing. PRSQ has him coming out of the shop before he has parked there. RPQS returns the bicycle before the theft has been reported.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Critics reply that such a charge would fall hardest on poorer drivers, who may have no other way to reach work.
(B) This is because a car entering a crowded road at rush hour slows every other vehicle on it, yet its driver pays nothing for that delay.
(C) Economists have long argued that drivers should pay for the congestion they cause.
(D) Supporters answer that the money raised could be spent on better buses, which poorer commuters use most.
(E) A fee for entering the busiest areas at peak hours would make drivers weigh that cost, and some would travel earlier, later or by bus.

solution.concept: Argument structure: claim → reason → proposal → objection → reply
solution.explanation: C states the economists' claim. B ('This is because') gives the reason. E proposes a fee that makes drivers weigh 'that cost'. A ('such a charge') is the critics' objection. D is the supporters' reply to it.
steps: C → B: 'This is because' explains it
B → E: the fee weighs 'that cost'
solution.why_others_wrong: CEBAD proposes the fee before explaining the cost it is meant to price. BCEAD opens with 'This is because', which needs a claim before it. CBEDA has supporters answering an objection that has not yet been raised.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Economists distinguish between a risk and an uncertainty.
(P) Such cases are much harder to insure, and markets often deal with them by spreading bets or by avoiding them altogether.
(Q) Insurers can price such situations, because past experience gives them a reliable guide to the future.
(R) An uncertainty, by contrast, is one in which even the chances cannot be calculated, such as whether an untried technology will succeed.
(S) A risk is a situation in which the possible outcomes and their chances are known, as when a fair die is rolled.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; define the first term → its consequence → contrast → its consequence
solution.explanation: S defines a risk. Q ('such situations') says insurers can price risks. R ('by contrast') defines an uncertainty. P ('Such cases') says uncertainties are hard to insure.
steps: S → Q: insurers can price risks
solution.why_others_wrong: SRQP makes Q's 'such situations' refer to uncertainties, which cannot be priced. RSQP gives 'by contrast' before the term it contrasts with. SQPR makes P's 'Such cases' refer to risks, which the passage says can be insured.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) As the days shorten in autumn, however, the tree stops making chlorophyll, and what remains breaks down.
(B) The reds, by contrast, are newly made in autumn, which is why their brightness varies from year to year with the weather.
(C) Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, which plants use to make food from sunlight.
(D) With the green gone, those hidden yellows and oranges show through.
(E) The leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments, but all summer these are masked by the green.

solution.concept: Para jumble: why green → hidden colours → loss of green → colours revealed → contrast with reds
solution.explanation: C explains the green colour. E ('also') adds the hidden yellows and oranges. A describes the loss of chlorophyll in autumn. D ('With the green gone') shows the hidden colours appearing. B ('by contrast') explains the reds, which were not hidden.
steps: A → D: hidden colours show → B: reds by contrast: CEADB
solution.why_others_wrong: CAEDB puts 'however' (autumn) straight after the plain fact about chlorophyll, with no summer state to contrast with, and removes the green before the hidden pigments are introduced. ECADB opens with 'also', which needs an earlier statement. CEABD puts the contrast with reds before the yellows and oranges have appeared.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) who sells vegetables
(Q) the woman
(R) is my neighbour's mother
(S) from a cart at the corner of our lane

solution.concept: Subject + relative clause (with its place phrase) + main verb
solution.explanation: 'The woman who sells vegetables from a cart at the corner of our lane is my neighbour's mother.' Subject (Q), relative clause (P) with its place phrase (S), then the main verb and complement (R).
solution.why_others_wrong: QRPS separates 'who sells vegetables' from 'the woman' and leaves the place phrase dangling at the end. PQSR opens with a relative clause that has no noun before it. QSPR gives 'the woman from a cart at the corner of our lane', cutting the place phrase off from 'sells vegetables'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) the more
(Q) you practise
(R) you will become
(S) the more confident

solution.concept: Double comparative: The more + clause, the more + adjective + clause
solution.explanation: 'The more you practise, the more confident you will become.' The first half is 'the more' (P) + 'you practise' (Q); the second is 'the more confident' (S) + 'you will become' (R).
solution.why_others_wrong: PSQR gives 'The more the more confident', which breaks the frame. SRPQ makes no sense as a statement. PRSQ gives 'The more you will become the more confident you practise', which reverses cause and result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) can the city
(Q) only by
(R) hope to reduce its traffic jams
(S) improving its bus service

solution.concept: Inversion after a fronted 'only by + -ing' phrase: Only by ... can + subject + verb
solution.explanation: 'Only by improving its bus service can the city hope to reduce its traffic jams.' The fronted phrase (Q + S) is followed by the inverted 'can the city' (P) and the rest of the verb (R).
steps: Fronted phrase: 'Only by' (Q) + 'improving its bus service' (S)
Rest of the verb: R → QSPR
solution.why_others_wrong: PRQS opens with an inverted question form and leaves 'only by improving' hanging at the end. QPSR splits 'only by' from 'improving'. SQPR puts 'improving its bus service' before 'only by'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The baby was so ______ after the long bus journey that she fell asleep in her mother's arms.

solution.concept: Single blank: the result clause ('so ... that she fell asleep') decides the word
solution.explanation: Falling asleep follows feeling sleepy. 'Drowsy' means sleepy.
solution.why_others_wrong: Being 'cheerful' or 'curious' does not lead to falling asleep, and 'restless' suggests the opposite.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Please ______ your seat belt; the plane is about to land.

solution.concept: Single blank: the fixed collocation 'fasten a seat belt'
solution.explanation: Before landing, passengers are asked to buckle their seat belts: 'fasten your seat belt'.
steps: Context: the plane is about to land
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Loosen' is the opposite of what is needed for landing. Seat belts are not 'lifted' or 'folded'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The village well had ______ up during the long, hot summer, so the women had to fetch water from the river.

solution.concept: Single blank: the phrasal verb 'dry up' and the result clause
solution.explanation: Water had to be fetched from the river because the well had no water left: it had 'dried up' in the heat.
steps: Result: water fetched from the river
Cause: no water in the well
solution.why_others_wrong: A well that had 'filled up' would remove the need to go to the river. 'Opened up' and 'cooled up' do not explain the lack of water.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The tailor ______ the trousers by two inches because they were too ______ for the boy.

solution.concept: Double blank: both words must agree with each other
solution.explanation: Trousers that are too long for the boy are made shorter: the tailor 'shortened' them because they were too 'long'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Lengthening long trousers or shortening short ones makes the problem worse. Stitching cannot fix a price.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The teacher asked the students to ______ the new words in their notebooks.

solution.concept: Phrase fillers: write down = record in writing
solution.explanation: Students record new words in notebooks: they 'write them down'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Give up' (stop), 'call off' (cancel) and 'run over' (knock down with a vehicle) make no sense with notebooks.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The fire alarm ______ suddenly in the middle of the night, and everyone rushed out of the building.

solution.concept: Phrase fillers: go off (of an alarm) = start ringing
solution.explanation: An alarm that starts ringing 'goes off', which is why everyone rushed out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Went over' (examined), 'went by' (passed) and 'went down' (fell or sank) do not describe an alarm ringing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The rumours about the minister's health proved ______; he was back at work the very next day.

solution.concept: Single blank: the clause after the semicolon gives the evidence
solution.explanation: If he was back at work the next day, the rumours that he was ill had no basis: they proved 'unfounded'.
steps: Evidence: back at work next day
solution.why_others_wrong: If the rumours were 'accurate', he would not be back at work. Rumours are not 'contagious' or 'permanent' in any sense that fits the evidence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The two neighbours have not been on ______ terms since their quarrel over the boundary wall, and they now ______ each other in the street.

solution.concept: Double blank: the idiom 'on speaking terms' and a consistent second word
solution.explanation: 'Not on speaking terms' means not talking to each other after a quarrel; such neighbours 'ignore' each other.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Talking terms' is not idiomatic, and greeting each other contradicts the quarrel. 'Help' and 'follow' do not fit people who have fallen out.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
Having been cheated once, the old man now tries to ______ anyone who promises to double his money.

solution.concept: Phrase fillers: steer clear of = deliberately avoid
solution.explanation: A man cheated before would avoid anyone making the same kind of promise: he 'steers clear of' them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Look up to' (admire) and 'catch up with' (reach) contradict his caution. 'Run short of' is used for supplies, not people.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Her ______ remarks, always delivered with a perfectly straight face, left the audience unsure whether she was joking.

solution.concept: Single blank: the description 'with a perfectly straight face' defines the word
solution.explanation: Humour delivered without any expression, so that listeners cannot tell whether it is a joke, is 'deadpan'.
steps: Clue: straight face, unsure if joking
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Effusive' remarks are full of open feeling, the opposite of a straight face. 'Rambling' describes length, not expression. 'Tearful' does not fit joking.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The minister's ______ promise to build a bridge, repeated at every election for twenty years, has become a local joke.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'repeated at every election for twenty years' points to something constantly recurring
solution.explanation: A promise that keeps coming back year after year is 'perennial' (lasting or recurring for a very long time).
solution.why_others_wrong: A promise repeated for twenty years is neither 'solitary' (single) nor 'sudden'. A 'sincere' promise kept unfulfilled for twenty years would hardly become a joke.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The film's ______ plot, full of improbable twists and half-explained flashbacks, ______ even its most loyal fans.

solution.concept: Double blank: the description in the middle decides both words
solution.explanation: A plot full of twists and half-explained flashbacks is 'convoluted' (complicated and hard to follow), and it would 'bewilder' (confuse) even loyal fans.
solution.why_others_wrong: A plot full of twists is neither 'lucid' (clear) nor 'predictable'. A 'gripping' plot would not disappoint its most loyal fans in this context.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
After five years of losses, the founder finally decided to ______ and sell the company to a larger rival.

solution.concept: Phrase fillers: cut one's losses = abandon a failing venture before losing more
solution.explanation: After five years of losses, selling the business stops the losses from growing: he 'cut his losses'.
steps: Action: sell to stop further loss
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Turn the tables' means reverse a situation in one's favour, which selling up is not. 'Hold his horses' means wait, and 'steal the show' means attract the most attention.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'breathe' used correctly?

options.text: The doctor asked the old man to breathe slowly and deeply.
She was out of breathe after climbing the stairs.
He held his breathe for a full minute under water.
Take a deep breathe before you dive into the water.

solution.concept: Breathe (verb, to take air in and out) vs breath (noun, the air taken in)
solution.explanation: 'Breathe' is a verb. 'To breathe slowly' uses it correctly as a verb after 'to'.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three need the noun 'breath': a deep breath, out of breath, held his breath.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The doctor asked the old man to breathe slowly and deeply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'personnel' used correctly?

options.text: She keeps her personnel diary locked in a drawer.
This is only my personnel opinion, not the company's.
All personnel must wear identity badges inside the factory.
He took a personnel interest in the new trainee's progress.

solution.concept: Personnel (noun, the people employed in an organisation) vs personal (adjective, one's own, private)
solution.explanation: 'Personnel' means the staff of an organisation. 'All personnel must wear identity badges' uses it correctly.
steps: 'All ___ must wear badges' = all staff → personnel: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three need the adjective 'personal' (one's own): personal opinion, personal diary, personal interest.
solution.final_answer: Option C: All personnel must wear identity badges inside the factory.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The hungry **(A) bone** chewed the **(B) dog** that the **(C) butcher** had thrown into the **(D) street**.

solution.concept: Word swap: check who can perform each action
solution.explanation: A bone cannot chew anything. Swapping A and B gives: 'The hungry dog chewed the bone that the butcher had thrown into the street.'
steps: The dog is the one that chews
solution.why_others_wrong: C-D gives 'the street had thrown into the butcher', which is absurd. B-C gives 'chewed the butcher', which leaves the bone as the one chewing. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'dessert' used correctly?

options.text: The camel caravan crossed the dessert in three days.
We had mango ice cream for dessert after dinner.
The soldier was punished for trying to dessert his post.
After the floods, the village looked dessert and empty.

solution.concept: Dessert (sweet dish after a meal) vs desert (dry land; or, as a verb, to abandon)
solution.explanation: 'Dessert' is the sweet course at the end of a meal. 'Mango ice cream for dessert after dinner' uses it correctly.
steps: Dry land crossed by camels → desert
Sweet course after dinner → dessert: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The camel sentence needs 'desert' (dry land), the soldier sentence the verb 'desert' (abandon), and the village sentence 'deserted'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: We had mango ice cream for dessert after dinner.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'morale' used correctly?

options.text: He is a man of high morale principles.
The story has a clear morale: honesty is always rewarded.
The surprise bonus lifted the morale of the tired staff.
It is our morale duty to help the flood victims.

solution.concept: Morale (spirit and confidence of a group) vs moral (a lesson; or, as an adjective, concerning right and wrong)
solution.explanation: 'Morale' means the confidence and spirit of a group. A bonus that cheers tired staff 'lifts their morale'.
steps: Spirit of the staff → morale: correct
Principles of right and wrong → moral
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three need 'moral': the moral of a story, moral principles, a moral duty.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The surprise bonus lifted the morale of the tired staff.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'allusion' used correctly?

options.text: He was under the allusion that the loan would be forgiven.
The magician created the allusion of a table floating in the air.
Her speech contained an allusion to the Salt March of 1930.
In the desert heat, the travellers saw an allusion of water.

solution.concept: Allusion (an indirect reference to something) vs illusion (a false idea or a deceptive appearance)
solution.explanation: An 'allusion' is a passing or indirect reference. A speech that refers to the Salt March contains an allusion to it.
steps: Magic trick that deceives the eye → illusion
Indirect reference in a speech → allusion: correct
A false belief → under the illusion
Water that is not really there → illusion
solution.why_others_wrong: The magic trick, the false belief and the imagined water are all deceptions, which need 'illusion'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Her speech contained an allusion to the Salt March of 1930.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) heavy** rain **(B) flooded** the low-lying **(C) fields** and **(D) washed** away the young crops.

solution.concept: Word swap: test each pair, and choose 'No swap' when the sentence already makes sense
solution.explanation: Heavy rain flooding low-lying fields and washing away young crops is perfectly sensible. No words need to be interchanged.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-C gives 'the fields rain ... heavy', B-D gives 'washed the fields and flooded away the crops', and A-B gives 'the flooded rain heavy'; each makes the sentence worse.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'reimburse' as used in the sentence:
'The company will reimburse the travel expenses of all candidates called for the interview.'

solution.concept: Reimburse = repay money that someone has spent
solution.explanation: Candidates pay their own fares to attend, and the company later returns that money to them: it reimburses them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Reduce' and 'check' do not mean returning money. 'Refuse' is the opposite of the company's promise.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Tenacious' and 'persistent' both mean holding on firmly and not giving up. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'unprecedented' as used in the sentence:
'The cyclone caused unprecedented damage; nothing like it had been seen on this coast for a hundred years.'

solution.concept: Unprecedented = without any earlier example
solution.explanation: The clause after the semicolon explains it: nothing like it had been seen in a hundred years. Damage with no earlier parallel is 'unprecedented'.
steps: Clue: nothing like it in a hundred years
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Expected and planned for' and 'small and easily repaired' contradict the clue. Nothing suggests the cyclone's damage was 'caused deliberately'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: never known or done before

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Zenith' is the highest point and 'nadir' the lowest point. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'insouciant' as used in the sentence:
'As the losses mounted month after month, the owner's insouciant attitude astonished his accountants.'

solution.concept: Insouciant = showing a casual lack of concern
solution.explanation: The accountants are astonished because the owner does not seem worried at all while losses mount. His attitude is 'insouciant': casually unconcerned.
solution.why_others_wrong: If he were 'deeply anxious' or 'quietly ashamed', his reaction would be normal and would not astonish anyone. Nothing suggests he was 'angrily defensive'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Landslides and heavy rain **impeded** the rescue work in the hills for two days.

solution.concept: Impede = obstruct or slow down
solution.explanation: Landslides and heavy rain make rescue work harder and slower: they 'impede' or 'hinder' it.
steps: Context: landslides and rain vs rescue work
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Assisted' is the opposite. Landslides do not 'announce' or 'inspect' work.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
She sat on the steps for an hour, **pensive**, wondering whether to accept the transfer.

solution.concept: Pensive = deep in serious thought
solution.explanation: Someone sitting for an hour wondering about a decision is lost in thought: 'pensive' or 'thoughtful'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cheerful', 'careless' and 'sleepy' do not describe someone weighing a decision.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The critic's **trenchant** review exposed every weakness in the play's script and acting.

solution.concept: Trenchant = vigorous and sharply incisive
solution.explanation: A review that exposes every weakness is sharp and forceful: 'trenchant', or 'cutting'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'flattering' review would hide weaknesses. 'Lengthy' refers to length, not sharpness. A 'confused' review could not expose every weakness clearly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The company's **profligate** spending on parties and foreign trips soon emptied its reserves.

solution.concept: Profligate = recklessly wasteful
solution.explanation: Spending on parties and trips that empties a company's reserves is recklessly wasteful: 'profligate', or 'extravagant'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Careful' and 'modest' spending would not empty the reserves. 'Secret' says nothing about how much was spent.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The new bridge is **sturdy** enough to carry heavily loaded lorries.

solution.concept: Sturdy = strong and solidly built; opposite: flimsy
solution.explanation: A bridge that can carry loaded lorries is strong. The opposite of 'sturdy' is 'flimsy' (weak, easily broken).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Strong' is a synonym, not an opposite. 'Long' and 'costly' describe size and price, not strength.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **vigilant** guard noticed the stranger loitering near the gate long before he tried to climb it.

solution.concept: Vigilant = keeping careful watch; opposite: inattentive
solution.explanation: The guard noticed the stranger early because he was watching carefully. The opposite of 'vigilant' is 'inattentive' (not paying attention).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Watchful' is a synonym. 'Armed' and 'elderly' describe the guard in other ways, not his attention.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The young founder's **audacious** plan to take on the market leader in its home city surprised investors.

solution.concept: Audacious = boldly daring; opposite: timorous
solution.explanation: Taking on the market leader in its home city is a bold, risky move. The opposite of 'audacious' is 'timorous' (timid, lacking courage).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Daring' is a synonym. 'Costly' and 'secret' describe other features of a plan, not its boldness.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Known for his **pugnacious** manner, the union leader picked a fight with almost everyone at the meeting.

solution.concept: Pugnacious = eager to quarrel or fight; opposite: peaceable
solution.explanation: A man who picks a fight with almost everyone is quarrelsome: 'pugnacious'. The opposite is 'peaceable' (inclined to avoid conflict).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Aggressive' is a synonym. 'Talkative' and 'wealthy' have nothing to do with quarrelling.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The **abstemious** old monk ate a single plain meal a day and never touched sweets.

solution.concept: Abstemious = sparing in eating and drinking; opposite: gluttonous
solution.explanation: Eating one plain meal a day and avoiding sweets is self-denying: 'abstemious'. The opposite is 'gluttonous' (eating far too much).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Frugal' is close in meaning, not opposite. 'Devout' and 'silent' describe religion and speech, not eating.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to pull someone's leg'.

solution.concept: Idiom: pull someone's leg = joke with someone by telling them something untrue
solution.explanation: To 'pull someone's leg' is to tease them in fun, for example by pretending something false is true.
solution.why_others_wrong: The idiom has nothing to do with hurting, helping someone walk or stopping them leaving; these read it literally.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to tease someone playfully

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold.
After walking home in the rain, Grandfather felt **under the weather** for a few days.

solution.concept: Idiom: under the weather = slightly ill
solution.explanation: After getting wet in the rain, Grandfather was a little ill for a few days: he felt 'under the weather'.
steps: Context: walked home in the rain
Result: a few days of feeling poorly
solution.why_others_wrong: Getting wet does not make one 'very cheerful', 'extremely busy' or 'short of money'; the idiom refers to health.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'a storm in a teacup'.

options.text: a sudden change in the weather
a quarrel that lasts for many years
a serious problem that is hidden from view
great anger or worry about a very small matter

solution.concept: Idiom: a storm in a teacup = a big fuss over something trivial
solution.explanation: A storm inside a teacup is tiny; the idiom describes a lot of excitement or anger about something unimportant.
steps: 'great anger or worry about a very small matter'
solution.why_others_wrong: The idiom is not about weather. A hidden serious problem is the opposite of a trivial one, and the idiom says nothing about a long-lasting quarrel.
solution.final_answer: Option D: great anger or worry about a very small matter

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best expresses the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Having resigned publicly and sold his house in the city, he had **burnt his boats**; there was no way back to his old job.

options.text: lost all his savings in a bad deal
travelled abroad in search of work
worked very hard to finish a task
made it impossible to return to his former position

solution.concept: Idiom: burn one's boats = take an action that makes retreat impossible
solution.explanation: The clause after the semicolon explains it: 'there was no way back'. By resigning publicly and selling his house, he had cut off any return.
solution.why_others_wrong: Losing savings, working hard and travelling abroad are not suggested; the context stresses only that he could not go back.
solution.final_answer: Option D: made it impossible to return to his former position

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'Achilles' heel'.

options.text: a reward given for great courage
an injury that heals very slowly
a small but serious weakness in someone otherwise strong
a habit of running away from danger

solution.concept: Idiom: Achilles' heel = a weak point that can lead to downfall
solution.explanation: In Greek legend, Achilles could be wounded only in his heel. The idiom means a single vulnerable point in a person or thing that is otherwise strong.
steps: Origin: Achilles, vulnerable only at the heel
solution.why_others_wrong: The idiom is not about slow healing, running away or a reward; those read the words literally or invent a meaning.
solution.final_answer: Option C: a small but serious weakness in someone otherwise strong

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
Able to speak two languages fluently

solution.concept: One-word substitution: bi- (two) + lingual (of language)
solution.explanation: 'Bilingual' means able to speak two languages fluently.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Eloquent' and 'articulate' mean able to express oneself well, in any number of languages. 'Literate' means able to read and write.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
An abnormal and extreme fear of heights

solution.concept: One-word substitution: acro- (height) + phobia (fear)
solution.explanation: 'Acrophobia' is an extreme fear of heights.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Claustrophobia' is fear of closed spaces, 'hydrophobia' fear of water, and 'xenophobia' fear or dislike of foreigners.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The members elected him secretary of the club.

options.text: He was elected by secretary of the club the members.
Secretary of the club was elected him by the members.
He has been elected secretary of the club by the members.
He was elected secretary of the club by the members.

solution.concept: Passive of a verb with an object and an object complement (elect, make, appoint + object + title)
solution.explanation: The object 'him' becomes the subject 'He'. The complement 'secretary of the club' stays after the verb. The tense is past simple: 'He was elected secretary of the club by the members.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Making 'Secretary' the subject turns the complement into the subject wrongly. 'Has been elected' changes the tense. 'He was elected by secretary of the club the members' scrambles the agent and the complement.
solution.final_answer: Option D: He was elected secretary of the club by the members.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
One should keep one's promises.

options.text: Promises are being kept by one.

solution.concept: Passive with a modal (should + be + past participle); a general 'one' as subject is dropped
solution.explanation: The object 'promises' becomes the subject. 'Should keep' becomes 'should be kept'. The general agent 'one' is left out: 'Promises should be kept.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Should have been kept' changes the time to the past. 'One's promises should keep' is active and changes the meaning. 'Are being kept by one' loses 'should' and keeps an awkward general agent.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Promises should be kept.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
She said, "I bought this saree yesterday."

options.text: She said that she bought this saree yesterday.
She said that she had bought that saree the previous day.
She said that I had bought that saree the previous day.
She said that she has bought that saree the day before.

solution.concept: Reported statement: past simple → past perfect; this → that; yesterday → the previous day
solution.explanation: With a past reporting verb, 'bought' moves back to 'had bought', 'I' becomes 'she', 'this' becomes 'that' and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.
steps: this → that; yesterday → the previous day
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping 'this' and 'yesterday' ignores the change of time and place. 'I had bought' keeps the wrong pronoun. 'Has bought' is present perfect, which does not follow 'said'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: She said that she had bought that saree the previous day.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
He said to me, "Will you lend me your bicycle for an hour?"

options.text: He asked me if I would lend me his bicycle for an hour.
He told me that I will lend him my bicycle for an hour.
He asked me if I would lend him my bicycle for an hour.
He asked me will I lend him my bicycle for an hour.

solution.concept: Reported yes/no question (a request): asked + if/whether + statement order; will → would
solution.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked' and 'if' (or 'whether') in statement order. 'Will' becomes 'would'; 'you' → 'I', 'me' → 'him', 'your' → 'my'.
steps: if + statement order: if I would lend
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Will I lend' keeps question order and the present 'will'. 'Told me that I will lend' turns the request into a statement. 'Lend me his bicycle' gets both pronouns wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He asked me if I would lend him my bicycle for an hour.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
She said, "Alas! I have lost my purse."

options.text: She exclaimed sorrowfully that she had lost her purse.
She exclaimed sorrowfully that she has lost my purse.
She said alas that she had lost her purse.
She exclaimed with joy that she had lost her purse.

solution.concept: Reported exclamation: the interjection becomes a reporting verb + adverb ('exclaimed sorrowfully'); present perfect → past perfect
solution.explanation: 'Alas' expresses sorrow, so the reporting verb becomes 'exclaimed sorrowfully' (or 'exclaimed with sorrow'). 'Have lost' → 'had lost', 'I' → 'she', 'my' → 'her'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping 'alas' inside the reported clause is wrong. 'Has lost my purse' keeps the wrong tense and pronoun. 'With joy' gets the feeling wrong: 'alas' expresses sorrow.
solution.final_answer: Option A: She exclaimed sorrowfully that she had lost her purse.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Ravi and his sister ______ to school by bus every day.

solution.concept: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Ravi and his sister' are two people, so the verb is plural. 'Every day' calls for the simple present: 'go'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Goes', 'is going' and 'has gone' are singular forms, and the last two also do not express a daily habit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Measles ______ a contagious disease that spreads quickly among children.

solution.concept: Names of diseases ending in -s (measles, mumps, rabies) are singular
solution.explanation: 'Measles' is the name of one disease and takes a singular verb: 'Measles is a contagious disease ...'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are', 'were' and 'have been' are plural forms, and 'were' also puts a general fact in the past.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
The rest of the mangoes ______ rotten, so the shopkeeper threw them away.

solution.concept: 'The rest of', like 'half of' and 'most of', agrees with the noun after 'of'
solution.explanation: 'The rest of the mangoes' refers to many mangoes, so the verb is plural. The story is in the past ('threw'), so it is 'were'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was', 'has been' and 'is' are singular; 'the rest of' + a singular noun ('the rest of the cake') would take them, but mangoes are plural.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
I ______ never ______ a tiger in the wild, though I have visited many forests.

solution.concept: Present perfect (have + past participle) for life experience up to now, often with 'never' or 'ever'
solution.explanation: The speaker is describing experience up to the present ('though I have visited many forests'), so the present perfect is used: 'I have never seen a tiger in the wild.'
steps: Time: whole life up to now
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Had' moves the time to before some past moment. 'Have saw' uses the past tense instead of the participle. 'Did seen' mixes the auxiliary 'did' with a participle.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Her eyes were red and she looked exhausted because she ______ all night.

solution.concept: Past perfect continuous: an activity that continued up to a past moment and explains a past result
solution.explanation: The red eyes and tiredness are a past result ('looked'). The activity that went on before it and caused it is in the past perfect continuous: 'because she had been studying all night.'
steps: Earlier, continuing activity: studying all night
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has been studying' is tied to the present and clashes with 'looked'. 'Is studying' is present. 'Was studied' is passive and makes no sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ Indian Ocean lies to the south of ______ India.

solution.concept: 'The' with the names of oceans and seas; no article with the names of most countries
solution.explanation: Oceans take 'the': 'the Indian Ocean'. Most country names take no article: 'India'. So: 'The Indian Ocean lies to the south of India.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No article, the' reverses the rule. 'The, the' wrongly puts 'the' before India. 'An Indian Ocean' would suggest one of several Indian oceans.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
______ Japanese are known all over the world for their politeness.

solution.concept: 'The' + a nationality adjective ending in -ese, -ch, -sh or -ss refers to the whole people
solution.explanation: Nationality words such as Japanese, Chinese, French and Swiss do not add -s in the plural. To refer to the people as a whole, they take 'the': 'The Japanese are known ... for their politeness.'
steps: Nationality in -ese: 'the' + adjective = the whole people
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A' and 'an' are singular and clash with 'are' and 'their'. Without an article, 'Japanese' would be read as the language or an adjective missing its noun.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The new science teacher is very popular ______ her students.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: popular with (a group of people)
solution.explanation: A person liked by a group is 'popular with' that group: 'The new science teacher is very popular with her students.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Popular by', 'popular to' and 'popular for' (the last is used for the reason, as in 'popular for her patience') do not fit before the people who like her.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The two brothers fell ______ over the division of their father's land and have not spoken since.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: fall out (with someone) = quarrel and stop being friendly
solution.explanation: The brothers quarrelled about the land and stopped speaking. To quarrel in this way is to 'fall out'.
steps: Context: dispute over land, not speaking since
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fall off' means decrease or drop from something. 'Fall through' means fail to happen (a plan). 'Fall back' means retreat. None means to quarrel.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
The chemist's shop was closed, ______ we went to the one across the road.

solution.concept: 'So' introduces a result
solution.explanation: Going to another shop is the result of the first shop being closed: 'The chemist's shop was closed, so we went to the one across the road.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'But' signals a contrast that is not there. 'Because' would make going across the road the reason the shop was closed. 'Unless' sets a condition that makes no sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
She studied very hard for the test, ______ she did not get the marks she had hoped for.

solution.concept: 'But' joins two facts that contrast
solution.explanation: Studying hard should bring good marks, yet she did not get them. The unexpected result is introduced by 'but'.
steps: Clause 2: did not get the marks (unexpected)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'So' would make hard work the cause of low marks. 'Because' reverses the logic. 'Unless' sets a condition that does not fit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
Please wait here ______ I come back with the tickets.

solution.concept: 'Until' = up to the time when
solution.explanation: The listener is to wait up to the moment the speaker returns: 'Please wait here until I come back with the tickets.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Unless' makes waiting depend on a condition that makes no sense. 'Although' and 'because' signal contrast and reason, which do not fit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
A landslide had blocked the main road; ______, the buses were sent through the next valley.

solution.concept: 'Hence' introduces a consequence
solution.explanation: Sending the buses by another route is a result of the main road being blocked, so the linker is 'hence' (= for this reason).
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Besides' adds a further point. 'Likewise' signals a similar action. 'Nevertheless' signals a contrast; none of these shows a result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Combine the two sentences into one without changing the meaning, and choose the correct combined sentence.
You can pay now. You can pay on delivery.

options.text: You can either pay now nor on delivery.
You can pay both now and on delivery.
You can pay neither now nor on delivery.
You can pay either now or on delivery.

solution.concept: 'Either ... or' joins two alternatives
solution.explanation: The two sentences give two choices of when to pay. Alternatives are joined by 'either ... or': 'You can pay either now or on delivery.'
steps: 'You can pay either now or on delivery.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Neither ... nor' denies both choices. 'Both ... and' means paying twice. 'Either ... nor' mixes two correlatives.
solution.final_answer: Option D: You can pay either now or on delivery.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that best fills the blank.
______ as it may seem, the cheaper option often costs more in the long run.

solution.concept: Concessive pattern: adjective + as + subject + verb (= although it may seem strange)
solution.explanation: 'Strange as it may seem' means 'although it may seem strange'. Only the bare adjective fits this pattern.
steps: Pattern: Adjective + as + it may seem
solution.why_others_wrong: 'So', 'too' and 'very' cannot stand before the adjective in this concessive pattern.
